claim: Budding yeast Spc110 is a member of the γ-tubulin complex receptor family (γ-TuCR).
source: Budding yeast Spc110, a member of γ-tubulin complex receptor family (γ-TuCR), recruits γ-tubulin complexes to microtubule (MT) organizing centers (MTOCs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of Spc110.

claim: Spc110 recruits γ-tubulin complexes to microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs).
source: Budding yeast Spc110, a member of γ-tubulin complex receptor family (γ-TuCR), recruits γ-tubulin complexes to microtubule (MT) organizing centers (MTOCs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a function of Spc110.

claim: Biochemical studies suggest that Spc110 facilitates higher-order γ-tubulin complex assembly.
source: Biochemical studies suggest that Spc110 facilitates higher-order γ-tubulin complex assembly (Kollman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Kollman et al., 2010.

claim: Spc110 phosphorylated by Mps1 and Cdk1 activates γ-TuSC oligomerization and MT nucleation in a cell cycle dependent manner.
source: Here we show that Spc110 phosphorylated by Mps1 and Cdk1 activates γ-TuSC oligomerization and MT nucleation in a cell cycle dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Interaction between the N-terminus of the γ-TuSC subunit Spc98 and Spc110 is important for γ-TuSC oligomerization and MT nucleation activity.
source: Interaction between the N-terminus of the γ-TuSC subunit Spc98 and Spc110 is important for this activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: The conserved CM1 motif in γ-TuCRs is important for MT nucleation.
source: Besides the conserved CM1 motif in γ-TuCRs (Sawin et al., 2004), a second motif that we named Spc110/Pcp1 motif (SPM) is also important for MT nucleation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract with citation to Sawin et al., 2004.

claim: A second motif named Spc110/Pcp1 motif (SPM) is important for MT nucleation.
source: Besides the conserved CM1 motif in γ-TuCRs (Sawin et al., 2004), a second motif that we named Spc110/Pcp1 motif (SPM) is also important for MT nucleation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: The activating Mps1 and Cdk1 sites lie between SPM and CM1 motifs.
source: The activating Mps1 and Cdk1 sites lie between SPM and CM1 motifs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Most organisms have both SPM-CM1 (Spc110/Pcp1/PCNT) and CM1-only (Spc72/Mto1/Cnn/CDK5RAP2/myomegalin) types of γ-TuCRs.
source: Most organisms have both SPM-CM1 (Spc110/Pcp1/PCNT) and CM1-only (Spc72/Mto1/Cnn/CDK5RAP2/myomegalin) types of γ-TuCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The two types of γ-TuCRs contain distinct but conserved C-terminal MTOC targeting domains.
source: The two types of γ-TuCRs contain distinct but conserved C-terminal MTOC targeting domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The budding yeast spindle consists of approximately 40 microtubules.
source: The budding yeast spindle consists of ∼40 microtubules (MTs) that extend between the two opposed spindle pole bodies (SPBs).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: In budding yeast, the SPBs remain embedded in the nuclear membrane throughout mitosis.
source: Because of the closed mitosis in yeast, the SPBs remain embedded in the nuclear membrane throughout mitosis.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Cell-cycle regulated spindle assembly begins in S-phase with nucleation of MTs onto the surface of the newly assembled SPB.
source: Cell-cycle regulated spindle assembly begins in S-phase with nucleation of MTs onto the surface of the newly assembled SPB.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: In budding yeast, two molecules of γ-tubulin (Tub4) assemble together with one molecule of Spc97 and Spc98 into a tetrameric γ-tubulin small complex (γ-TuSC).
source: In budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, two molecules of γ-tubulin (Tub4) assemble together with one molecule of Spc97 (ortholog of human GCP2) and Spc98 (ortholog of human GCP3) into a tetrameric γ-tubulin small complex (γ-TuSC), which is conserved in all eukaryotes (Geissler et al., 1996; Knop et al., 1997; Guillet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The γ-TuSC is conserved in all eukaryotes.
source: In budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, two molecules of γ-tubulin (Tub4) assemble together with one molecule of Spc97 (ortholog of human GCP2) and Spc98 (ortholog of human GCP3) into a tetrameric γ-tubulin small complex (γ-TuSC), which is conserved in all eukaryotes (Geissler et al., 1996; Knop et al., 1997; Guillet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The purified γ-TuSC of budding yeast is able to self-oligomerize into symmetric ring-like structures under low salt buffer conditions.
source: The purified γ-TuSC of budding yeast is able to self-oligomerize into symmetric ring-like structures under low salt buffer conditions.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: The diameter and the pitch of the γ-TuSC ring resemble that of MT cylinder.
source: The diameter and the pitch of the γ-TuSC ring resemble that of MT cylinder, suggesting that the γ-TuSC ring functions as a MT nucleation template.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: The in vitro nucleation activity of the γ-TuSC assemblies remained poor, presumably because of the suboptimal spacing of every second Tub4 within the γ-TuSC ring.
source: However, the in vitro nucleation activity of the γ-TuSC assemblies remained poor, presumably because of the suboptimal spacing of every second Tub4 within the γ-TuSC ring that blocks interaction with tubulin in the MT cylinder (Kollman et al., 2008, 2010; Choy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: In vivo measurements of budding yeast γ-tubulin complex components on detached single MT nucleation sites showed a γ-tubulin:Spc97:Spc98 ratio of 2.4:1.0:1.3 with a total of approximately 17 γ-tubulin molecules per nucleation site.
source: The concept of γ-TuSC oligomerization is further supported by in vivo measurements of budding yeast γ-tubulin complex components on detached single MT nucleation sites. The γ-tubulin:Spc97:Spc98 ratio was 2.4:1.0:1.3 with a total of ∼17 γ-tubulin molecules per nucleation site (Erlemann et al., 2012), suggesting a slight excess of γ-tubulin and Spc98 molecules over Spc97 in the assembled MT nucleation site.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Erlemann et al., 2012.

claim: In most eukaryotic organisms, multiple γ-TuSCs further assemble with additional GCP family members (GCP4-6) into the larger γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC).
source: In most eukaryotic organisms, such as fission yeast, Drosophila, Xenopus, and human, multiple γ-TuSCs further assemble with additional GCP family members (GCP4-6) into the larger γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) (Gunawardane et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2000; Murphy et al., 2001; Anders et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Additional GCP proteins (GCP4-6) are not encoded in the budding yeast genome.
source: However, these additional GCP proteins are not encoded in the budding yeast genome.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Mozart1 is encoded in most eukaryotic genomes except the one of budding yeast.
source: The small protein Mozart1 is encoded in most eukaryotic genomes except the one of budding yeast (Teixido-Travesa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Teixido-Travesa et al., 2012.

claim: In Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Arabidopsis thaliana, Mozart1 interacts with the GCP3 subunit of γ-tubulin complexes.
source: In Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Arabidopsis thaliana Mozart1 interacts with the GCP3 subunit of γ-tubulin complexes (Janski et al., 2012; Nakamura et al., 2012; Batzenschlager et al., 2013; Dhani et al., 2013; Masuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: In S. pombe, Mozart1 appears important for the γ-TuSC recruitment to SPBs.
source: In S. pombe Mozart1 appears important for the γ-TuSC recruitment to SPBs (Dhani et al., 2013; Masuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Most γ-tubulin complex receptors carry a highly conserved centrosomin motif 1 (CM1) that interacts with GCP subunits of γ-tubulin complexes.
source: Most of them carry a highly conserved centrosomin motif 1 (CM1) that interacts with GCP subunits of γ-tubulin complexes (Sawin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Sawin et al., 2004.

claim: In budding yeast cells that lack a Mozart1 gene, γ-TuCRs are the sole factors responsible for γ-TuSC recruitment to SPBs.
source: However, in budding yeast cells that lack a Mozart1 gene, γ-TuCRs are the sole factors responsible for γ-TuSC recruitment to SPBs.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Spc110 is the budding yeast homolog of pericentrin (PCNT) and functions as γ-TuCRs at the nuclear side of the SPB.
source: Spc110 is the budding yeast homolog of pericentrin (PCNT) and functions as γ-TuCRs at the nuclear side of the SPB (Knop and Schiebel, 1997; Sundberg and Davis, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The N-terminal Spc110 encompasses the CM1 that interacts with the Spc98 subunit of γ-TuSC.
source: The N-terminal Spc110 encompasses the CM1 that interacts with the Spc98 subunit of γ-TuSC (Knop and Schiebel, 1997; Nguyen et al., 1998; Vinh et al., 2002; Sawin et al., 2004; Zhang and Megraw, 2007; Fong et al., 2008; Samejima et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The N-terminal region of Spc110 is phosphorylated in a cell-cycle dependent manner.
source: In addition, the N-terminal region of Spc110 is phosphorylated in a cell-cycle dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Phospho-Spc110 appears as cells progress from S phase, continues accumulating during mitosis, and vanishes at the anaphase onset.
source: Phospho-Spc110 appears as cells progress from S phase, continues accumulating during mitosis, and vanishes at the anaphase onset (Friedman et al., 1996; Stirling and Stark, 1996).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Spc110 phosphorylation accounts for the impact of Cdk1 and Mps1 kinases on spindle dynamics.
source: Spc110 phosphorylation accounts for the impact of Cdk1 and Mps1 kinases on spindle dynamics (Friedman et al., 2001; Huisman et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: When γ-TuSC and an N-terminal fragment of Spc110 (amino acids 1–220) were co-expressed in insect cells, a filament-like γ-TuSC-Spc110(1–220) complex formed.
source: Interestingly, when γ-TuSC and an N-terminal fragment of Spc110 (amino acids 1–220 of Spc110; Spc1101–220) were co-expressed in insect cells, a filament-like γ-TuSC-Spc1101–220 complex formed.
evidence: This is stated with reference to prior work by Kollman et al., 2010.

claim: The nucleation capacity of purified γ-TuSC-Spc110(1–220) complex exceeded that of the γ-TuSC alone.
source: The nucleation capacity of this purified γ-TuSC-Spc1101–220 complex exceeded that of the γ-TuSC alone (Kollman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Kollman et al., 2010.

claim: Spc110(1–220) purified from insect cells harboured phosphorylations on S60/T68 and S36/S91, corresponding to established Mps1 and Cdk1 sites.
source: Because of the post-translational modification machinery, Spc1101–220 purified from insect cells harboured phosphorylations on S60/T68 and S36/S91 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D), that correspond to established Mps1 and Cdk1 sites, respectively (Figure 1A; Friedman et al., 2001; Huisman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D and citations to prior work.

claim: Spc110(1–220) was not phosphorylated when purified from E. coli.
source: In contrast, Spc1101–220 was not phosphorylated when purified from E. coli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Phosphorylated Spc110(1–220) from insect cells induced an apparent shift of γ-TuSC towards the void-volume in gel filtration compared to γ-TuSC alone.
source: Addition of Spc1101–220-P shifted γ-TuSC into fractions that eluted earlier than when γ-TuSC was run on the columns on its own (Figure 1B, shift from fraction 10 to fraction 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1B showing gel filtration data.

claim: Non-phosphorylated Spc110(1–220) expressed in E. coli did not change the γ-TuSC elution profile in gel filtration.
source: In contrast, non-phosphorylated Spc1101–220 expressed in E. coli did not change the γ-TuSC elution profile. The γ-TuSC pool eluted as monomeric γ-TuSC (Figure 1B, fractions 10–11).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1B showing gel filtration data.

claim: Phosphorylation of Spc110(1–220) alters the interaction with γ-TuSC.
source: This result suggests that Mps1 and Cdk1 kinases regulate the interaction between Spc110 and γ-TuSC through phosphorylation of Spc110 N-terminal domain.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the gel filtration results.

claim: The phosphomimetic Spc110(1–220)-2D (Cdk1 sites: S36D and S91D) induced an apparent shift of γ-TuSC towards the void-volume in gel filtration.
source: The phosphomimetic Spc1101–220-2D (Cdk1 sites), Spc1101–220-3D (Mps1 sites), and Spc1101–220-5D (Cdk1 and Mps1 sites) induced an apparent shift of γ-TuSC towards the void-volume compared to the γ-TuSC only run or γ-TuSC plus non-phosphorylated Spc1101–220-WT from E. coli (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B showing gel filtration data.

claim: The phosphomimetic Spc110(1–220)-3D (Mps1 sites: S60D, T64D, T68D) induced an apparent shift of γ-TuSC towards the void-volume in gel filtration.
source: The phosphomimetic Spc1101–220-2D (Cdk1 sites), Spc1101–220-3D (Mps1 sites), and Spc1101–220-5D (Cdk1 and Mps1 sites) induced an apparent shift of γ-TuSC towards the void-volume compared to the γ-TuSC only run or γ-TuSC plus non-phosphorylated Spc1101–220-WT from E. coli (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B showing gel filtration data.

claim: The phosphomimetic Spc110(1–220)-5D (Cdk1 and Mps1 sites: S36D, S60D, T64D, T68D, and S91D) induced an apparent shift of γ-TuSC towards the void-volume in gel filtration.
source: The phosphomimetic Spc1101–220-2D (Cdk1 sites), Spc1101–220-3D (Mps1 sites), and Spc1101–220-5D (Cdk1 and Mps1 sites) induced an apparent shift of γ-TuSC towards the void-volume compared to the γ-TuSC only run or γ-TuSC plus non-phosphorylated Spc1101–220-WT from E. coli (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B showing gel filtration data.

claim: The non-phosphorylatable Spc110(1–220)-5A (Cdk1 and Mps1 sites) did not induce γ-TuSC shift in gel filtration.
source: In contrast, the γ-TuSC shift was not seen upon inclusion of non-phosphorylatable Spc1101–220-5A (Cdk1 and Mps1 sites) with the γ-TuSC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B showing gel filtration data.

claim: Phosphorylated Spc110 induces oligomerization of γ-TuSC.
source: Taken together, the gel filtration experiment suggests that phosphorylated Spc110 induces oligomerization of γ-TuSC.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the gel filtration experiments.

claim: Oligomeric γ-TuSC ring-like assemblies were observed when Spc110(1–220)-2D, Spc110(1–220)-3D, and Spc110(1–220)-5D had been added to the γ-TuSC preparation.
source: In contrast, oligomeric γ-TuSC ring-like assemblies were observed when Spc1101–220-2D, Spc1101–220-3D, and Spc1101–220-5D (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B) had been added to the γ-TuSC preparation.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B showing EM images.

claim: The percentage of γ-TuSC spirals increased steadily with increasing numbers of phosphomimetic mutations from Spc110(1–220)-2D, Spc110(1–220)-3D to Spc110(1–220)-5D.
source: Interestingly, the percentage of γ-TuSC spirals increased steadily with increasing numbers of phosphomimetic mutations from Spc1101–220-2D, Spc1101–220-3D to Spc1101–220-5D (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), while the number of rings per field was relatively constant (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C showing quantification of EM data.

claim: The outer diameter of the ring-like γ-TuSC assemblies was on average around 40 nm.
source: The outer diameter of the ring-like assemblies was on average around 40 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4D showing quantification of EM data.

claim: Combined phosphorylation of Spc110 by Cdk1 and Mps1 kinases enhances the oligomerization activity of Spc110 better than phosphorylation by either kinase alone.
source: Thus, combined phosphorylation of Spc110 by Cdk1 and Mps1 kinases enhances the oligomerization activity of Spc110 better than phosphorylation by either kinase alone.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the EM analysis.

claim: T18 of Spc110 has been identified as a phosphorylation site in phosphoproteomic studies.
source: An additional phosphorylation of N-Spc110 at T18 has been identified in phosphoproteomic studies (Albuquerque et al., 2008; Keck et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Spc110(1–220) species with T18D or T18A failed to induce γ-TuSC oligomerization even when combined with the activating 5D mutations.
source: Spc1101–220 species with T18D or T18A failed to induce γ-TuSC oligomerization even when combined with the activating 5D mutations (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C showing gel filtration data.

claim: spc110T18D, spc110T18E, spc110T18A, and spc110T18V showed identical growth defects at 37°C.
source: Moreover, spc110T18D, spc110T18E, spc110T18A, and spc110T18V showed identical growth defects at 37°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 5B showing growth assay data.

claim: T18 mutations affect the structure of an important element around T18 that is important for γ-TuSC oligomerization.
source: However, our results strongly suggest that these mutations affect the structure of an important yet unappreciated element around T18 that is important for γ-TuSC oligomerization.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the T18 mutation data.

claim: A conserved motif upstream of CM1, designated as Spc110/Pcp1 motif (SPM), was observed in sequence alignments of Spc110 orthologs from yeast to human.
source: With the sequence alignments of Spc110 orthologs from yeast to human, we observed a conserved motif upstream of CM1, which we designated as Spc110/Pcp1 motif (SPM) (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2H showing sequence alignment.

claim: Spc110T18 sits within the SPM motif.
source: Spc110T18 sits within this motif.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Spc110(1–220)-5D-CM1-QA mutant protein failed to activate γ-TuSC oligomerization.
source: Spc1101–220-5D-CM1-QA and Spc1101–220-5D-ΔSPM mutant proteins failed to activate γ-TuSC oligomerization even when the five activating Cdk1 and Mps1 mutations were present (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2I showing gel filtration data.

claim: Spc110(1–220)-5D-ΔSPM mutant protein failed to activate γ-TuSC oligomerization.
source: Spc1101–220-5D-CM1-QA and Spc1101–220-5D-ΔSPM mutant proteins failed to activate γ-TuSC oligomerization even when the five activating Cdk1 and Mps1 mutations were present (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2I showing gel filtration data.

claim: SPM and CM1 of Spc110 are both required for γ-TuSC oligomerization.
source: Taken together, SPM and CM1 of Spc110 are both required for γ-TuSC oligomerization.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the SPM and CM1 mutant analysis.

claim: Spc110(1–220)-5D showed stronger γ-TuSC binding than Spc110(1–220)-WT in GST-pulldown assay.
source: Consistent with the γ-TuSC oligomerization assay (Figure 2), Spc1101–220-5D showed stronger (p=0.0017 for Spc97/Spc98 and p=0.0006 for Tub4) γ-TuSC binding than Spc1101–220-WT (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3A,B showing GST-pulldown data.

claim: Phosphorylation of Spc110 on S36, S60, T64, T68, and S91 promotes γ-TuSC binding to Spc110.
source: These results suggested that phosphorylation of Spc110 on S36, S60, T64, T68, and S91 promotes γ-TuSC binding to Spc110.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the GST-pulldown data.

claim: Both Spc110(1–220)-5D-T18D and Spc110(1–220)-5D-CM1-QA exhibited reduced γ-TuSC binding relative to Spc110(1–220)-5D.
source: Both Spc1101–220-5D-T18D and Spc1101–220-5D-CM1-QA exhibited reduced γ-TuSC binding relative to Spc1101–220-5D (p<0.01 for Spc97/Spc98 and p<0.05 for Tub4) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3C,D showing GST-pulldown data.

claim: The γ-TuSC binding capacity of Spc110(1–220)-5D-T18D-CM1-QA was further reduced compared to single mutants.
source: The γ-TuSC binding capacity of Spc1101–220-5D-T18D-CM1-QA was further reduced (p<0.01, Figure 3C,D), suggesting both CM1 and SPM are important for γ-TuSC binding.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 3C,D showing GST-pulldown data.

claim: Both CM1 and SPM motifs contribute to γ-TuSC binding and are required for promoting γ-TuSC oligomerization.
source: Taken together, we conclude that both CM1 and SPM motifs contribute to γ-TuSC binding and are required for promoting γ-TuSC oligomerization.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the binding and oligomerization data.

claim: A threefold increase in MT nucleation activity was observed for Spc110(1–220)-2D, Spc110(1–220)-3D, or Spc110(1–220)-5D upon incubation with γ-TuSC compared to buffer control and γ-TuSC alone.
source: Compared to the buffer control and γ-TuSC alone, a ∼threefold increase (p<0.05) in MT nucleation activity was observed for Spc1101–220-2D, Spc1101–220-3D, or Spc1101–220-5D upon incubation with γ-TuSC (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 4A,B showing MT nucleation assay data.

claim: Spc110(1–220)-WT showed levels of MT nucleation that were comparable to the buffer control and γ-TuSC alone.
source: In contrast, Spc1101–220-WT showed levels of MT nucleation that were comparable to the buffer control and γ-TuSC alone.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The MT nucleation level was reduced to buffer control levels when Spc110(1–220)-5D-T18D was incubated with γ-TuSC.
source: Consistent with the proposed role of SPM, the MT nucleation level was reduced to buffer control levels when Spc1101–220-5D-T18D was incubated with γ-TuSC (p=0.99).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Cdk1 and Mps1 phosphorylations of Spc110 regulate γ-TuSC-mediated MT nucleation by controlling template assembly.
source: In summary, these data support the model that Cdk1 and Mps1 phosphorylations of Spc110 regulate γ-TuSC-mediated MT nucleation by controlling template assembly.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the MT nucleation assay data.

claim: Spc110S36 and Spc110S91 were phosphorylated equally by Cdk1-Clb2 and Cdk1-Clb5 in vitro.
source: Spc110S36-S91 was phosphorylated equally by Cdk1-Clb2 and Cdk1-Clb5 as detected by Spc110pS36-pS91 antibodies (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 5A showing in vitro kinase assay data.

claim: At G1 phase, no signal was observed with any of the two phospho-specific antibodies (anti-Spc110pS36-pS91 and anti-Spc110pS60-pT64-pT68).
source: At G1 phase, no signal was observed with any of the two phospho-specific antibodies (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 5D showing immunoblot data.

claim: The phosphorylation of Mps1 sites on Spc110 was detected at S phase and maintained in mitosis.
source: The phosphorylation of Mps1 was detected at S phase and maintained in mitosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The Spc110pS36-pS91 signal appeared at S phase and continuously increased in mitosis.
source: The Spc110pS36-pS91 signal also appeared at S phase, and continuously increased in mitosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: T18 of Spc110 was only phosphorylated by Cdk1-Clb2 but not by Cdk1-Clb5 in vitro.
source: In vitro phosphorylation assay showed that T18 was only phosphorylated by Cdk1-Clb2 but not by Cdk1-Clb5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing in vitro kinase assay data.

claim: pT18 was predominately detected in the SPB-containing pellet fraction of prometaphase cells but not in the corresponding fraction of G1 or S phase arrested cells.
source: pT18 was predominately detected in the SPB-containing pellet fraction of prometaphase cells but not in the corresponding fraction of G1 or S phase arrested cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C showing mass spectrometry data.

claim: T18 of Spc110 becomes phosphorylated at SPBs in M phase but not S phase.
source: These data suggest that T18 of Spc110 becomes phosphorylated at SPBs in M phase but not S phase, which is consistent with published data (Keck et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mass spectrometry data with citation to prior work.

claim: In vitro phosphorylation of T18 by Cdk1-Clb2 inhibits γ-TuSC oligomerization.
source: This suggests that in vitro phosphorylation of T18 by Cdk1-Clb2 inhibits γ-TuSC oligomerization.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the gel filtration data with in vitro phosphorylated Spc110.

claim: The Cdk1 (S36, S91) and Mps1 sites of Spc110 become phosphorylated in S and in mitosis.
source: Taken together, our results are in agreement with previous reports about the timing of Spc110 phospho-dependent mobility shift in SDS-PAGE (Friedman et al., 1996; Stirling and Stark, 1996) and suggest that the Cdk1 (S36, S91) and Mps1 sites become phosphorylated in S and in mitosis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the phosphorylation timing data with citations to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of T18 within SPM occurs in mitosis and may negatively regulate SPM function.
source: In addition, phosphorylation of T18 within SPM occurs in mitosis and may negatively regulate SPM function.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the T18 phosphorylation data.

claim: spc110T18D and spc110ΔSPM cells displayed a conditional lethal growth defect at 37°C.
source: However, spc110T18D and spc110ΔSPM cells displayed a conditional lethal growth defect at 37°C and the SPM/CM1 defective spc110T18D-CM1-QA double mutant was non-viable at 23°C and 37°C (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6A showing growth assay data.

claim: The spc110T18D-CM1-QA double mutant was non-viable at 23°C and 37°C.
source: However, spc110T18D and spc110ΔSPM cells displayed a conditional lethal growth defect at 37°C and the SPM/CM1 defective spc110T18D-CM1-QA double mutant was non-viable at 23°C and 37°C (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6A showing growth assay data.

claim: Combining T18D with 2D (Cdk1 sites), 3D (Mps1 sites) and 5D mutations slightly reduced growth at 37°C compared to the 2D, 3D, and 5D mutations.
source: Combining T18D with 2D (Cdk1 sites), 3D (Mps1 sites) and 5D mutations slightly reduced growth at 37°C compared to the 2D, 3D, and 5D mutations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6A showing growth assay data.

claim: The SPM mutation T18D is dominant over the activating Cdk1 and Mps1 phosphomimetic mutations.
source: This shows that, consistent with our in vitro γ-TuSC oligomerization results (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), the SPM mutation T18D is dominant over the activating Cdk1 and Mps1 phosphomimetic mutations.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the growth assay data.

claim: In SPM defective spc110T18A and spc110T18D cells, the reduction of GFP-tubulin signal at SPBs was already apparent in G1.
source: In SPM defective spc110T18A and spc110T18D cells, the reduction of GFP-tubulin signal at SPBs was already apparent in G1 (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, p<0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: In S phase, all spc110 mutants except for spc1105D cells exhibited a marked reduction in MT nucleation at SPBs when compared with WT cells.
source: In S phase, the stage where newly synthesized SPBs mature and MT nucleation is initiated, all spc110 mutants except for spc1105D cells exhibited a marked reduction in MT nucleation at SPBs when compared with WT cells (Figure 6B; for spc1105A, p<0.05; for spc110T18D, spc110T18A, p<0.001; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The overall spindle MT signal was reduced in spc1105A, spc110T18A, spc110T18D, and spc1105D-T18D cells in metaphase.
source: Consistently, the overall spindle MT signal was reduced in spc1105A, spc110T18A, spc110T18D, and spc1105D-T18D cells (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6B,C showing fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The SPB signal from the γ-TuSC marker Spc97-GFP was reduced in spc1105A, spc110T18D, spc1105D-T18D, and spc110ΔSPM cells in G1 and S phase compared to SPC110WT and spc1105D cells.
source: We found that the SPB signal from the γ-TuSC marker Spc97-GFP was reduced in spc1105A, spc110T18D, spc1105D-T18D, and spc110ΔSPM cells in G1 and S phase compared to SPC110WT and spc1105D cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,G showing fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: MT nucleation activity was reduced in the spc1105A, spc110T18A, spc110T18D spc1105D-T18D cells compared to WT and spc1105D cells in the in vivo MT nucleation assay.
source: In comparison to WT and spc1105D cells, MT nucleation activity was reduced in the spc1105A, spc110T18A, spc110T18D spc1105D-T18D cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 6E showing in vivo MT nucleation assay data.

claim: Spc110's ability to stimulate MT nucleation is regulated through stimulatory phosphorylation and requires the SPM motif.
source: Again, these data are consistent with the in vitro data (Figures 1–4) and suggest that Spc110's ability to stimulate MT nucleation is regulated through stimulatory phosphorylation and requires the SPM motif.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the in vivo MT nucleation assay data.

claim: The N-terminal region of Spc98/GCP3 orthologs is conserved.
source: The N-terminal region of Spc98/GCP3 orthologs is conserved.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Spc98/GCP3 family members contain five predicted helices followed by an unstructured linker region.
source: Spc98/GCP3 family members contain five predicted helices followed by an unstructured linker region (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A showing sequence alignment and structure prediction.

claim: All N-terminal truncations of SPC98 supported cell growth at 23°C.
source: All N-terminal truncations of SPC98 supported cell growth at 23°C (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing growth assay data.

claim: Δ1–156, Δ1–177, and ΔLinker deletions of SPC98 showed reduced or no growth in mad2Δ cells at 37°C.
source: However, Δ1–156, Δ1–177, and ΔLinker deletions of SPC98 showed reduced or no growth in mad2Δ cells at 37°C.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: spc98Δ1–156 cells incubated at 37°C had weaker GFP-Tub1 signal at their SPBs than wild type SPC98 cells.
source: spc98Δ1–156 cells incubated at 37°C had weaker GFP-Tub1 signal at their SPBs than wild type SPC98 cells (WT, Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 7C showing fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Spc110(1–220)-5D failed to shift γ-TuSC(Spc98Δ1–156) to the void volume of the Superose 6 column.
source: Interestingly, Spc1101–220-5D failed to shift γ-TuSCSpc98Δ1–156 to the void volume of the Superose 6 column, as was the case for γ-TuSC (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 7E showing gel filtration data.

claim: γ-TuSC(Spc98Δ1–156) showed reduced binding to Spc110(1–220)-5D in the pull down assay.
source: In agreement with the oligomerization experiment, γ-TuSCSpc98Δ1–156 showed reduced binding to Spc1101–220-5D in the pull down assay (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 7F,G showing GST-pulldown data.

claim: The N-terminus of Spc98 is involved in binding to Spc110.
source: Thus, the N-terminus of Spc98 is involved in binding to Spc110.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the binding and oligomerization data with Spc98Δ1–156.

claim: γ-TuSC and γ-TuSC(Spc98Δ1–156) shifted to the void volume of the Superose 6 column with equal efficiency in BRB80 buffer.
source: γ-TuSC and γ-TuSCSpc98Δ1–156 shifted to the void volume of the Superose 6 column with equal efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C showing gel filtration data.

claim: The N-terminus of Spc98 is important for Spc110-mediated oligomerization but not for Spc110-independent γ-TuSC oligomerization.
source: Therefore, the N-terminus of Spc98 is important for Spc110-mediated oligomerization but not for Spc110-independent γ-TuSC oligomerization.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the oligomerization data with Spc98Δ1–156.

claim: A yet unappreciated CM1 motif was identified in another budding yeast γ-TuCR, Spc72.
source: A yet unappreciated CM1 motif was identified in another budding yeast γ-TuCR, Spc72 (Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C showing sequence alignment.

claim: Based on the presence of SPM and CM1 motifs, γ-TuCRs can be divided into the SPM-CM1 and the CM1-only types.
source: Based on the presence of SPM and CM1 motifs, γ-TuCRs can be divided into the SPM-CM1 and the CM1-only types.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Spc110 and fission yeast Pcp1 fall into the SPM-CM1 class of γ-TuCRs.
source: Spc110 and fission yeast Pcp1 fall into the SPM-CM1 class.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis predicts SPM and CM1 motifs in mammalian PCNT.
source: Our analysis also predicts SPM and CM1 motifs, albeit with moderate sequence deviation, in mammalian PCNT (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 8B showing bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Human CDK5RAP2 and myomegalin, Drosophila Cnn, budding yeast Spc72, and fission yeast Mto1 fall into the CM1-only class of γ-TuCRs.
source: Human CDK5RAP2 and myomegalin, Drosophila Cnn, budding yeast Spc72, and fission yeast Mto1 fall into this class (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 8B showing bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Yeast Spc110, Pcp1, Drosophila D-PLP (Cp309), and mammalian PCNT are targeted to nuclear side of SPBs or centrosomal MTOCs via the conserved PACT domain.
source: It was shown that yeast Spc110 (Sundberg et al., 1996; Stirling and Stark, 2000), Pcp1 (Fong et al., 2010), Drosophila D-PLP (Cp309) (Kawaguchi and Zheng, 2004), and mammalian PCNT (Gillingham and Munro, 2000; Takahashi et al., 2002) are targeted to nuclear side of SPBs or centrosomal MTOCs via the conserved PACT domain (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 9A.

claim: SPM-CM1 γ-TuCRs only function in organizing the nuclear MTs that separate the sister chromatids in mitosis in organisms with SPBs embedded in the nuclear envelope.
source: In case of SPBs that are embedded in the nuclear envelope and therefore have a cytoplasmic and a nuclear side, SPM-CM1 γ-TuCRs only function in organizing the nuclear MTs that separate the sister chromatids in mitosis (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 9B showing a summary diagram.

claim: CM1-only γ-TuCRs of fungi, such as Spc72 in budding yeast, Mto1 in fission yeast, and ApsB in Aspergillus nidulans, have a MASC motif and function at the cytoplasmic side of the SPB or in the cytoplasm.
source: In contrast, CM1-only γ-TuCRs of fungi, such as Spc72 in budding yeast (Knop and Schiebel, 1998), Mto1 in fission yeast (Samejima et al., 2010), and ApsB in Aspergillus nidulans (Zekert et al., 2010), have a MASC motif and function at the cytoplasmic side of the SPB or in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to prior work.

claim: In metazoa, CM1-only type of γ-TuCRs such as CDK5RAP2 possess a CM2 domain, targeting γ-TuCRs to both centrosomal and acentrosomal MTOCs.
source: In case of metazoa, CM1-only type of γ-TuCRs such as CDK5RAP2 (Wang et al., 2010) possess a CM2 domain (Figure 9B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), targeting γ-TuCRs to both centrosomal and acentrosomal MTOCs.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to prior work and reference to Figure 9B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: γ-TuCR family proteins can be classified regarding the γ-TuSC interaction motifs and the MTOC targeting domain into three groups.
source: In summary, γ-TuCR family proteins can be classified regarding the γ-TuSC interaction motifs and the MTOC targeting domain into three groups.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Spc110 is a MT nucleation regulator.
source: Thus, Spc110 is a MT nucleation regulator.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Binding of γ-TuSC to Spc110 is a prerequisite for γ-TuSC oligomerization into the ring-like template that initiates MT assembly.
source: Binding of γ-TuSC to Spc110 is a prerequisite for γ-TuSC oligomerization into the ring-like template that initiates MT assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Phosphorylation of Spc110 by Cdk1 and Mps1 regulates γ-TuSC binding and thereby MT nucleation.
source: Phosphorylation of Spc110 by Cdk1 and Mps1 regulates γ-TuSC binding and thereby MT nucleation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: In late G1, a SPB precursor, named the duplication plaque, assembles on the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope at a specialized substructure of the mother SPB, named bridge.
source: In late G1, a SPB precursor, named the duplication plaque, assembles on the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope at a specialized substructure of the mother SPB, named bridge (Byers and Goetsch, 1975; Jaspersen and Winey, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: In G1/S the duplication plaque becomes inserted into the nuclear envelope.
source: In G1/S the duplication plaque then becomes inserted into the nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: In G1/S phase, Mps1 and Cdk1-Clb5 phosphorylate the N-terminus of Spc110 at five sites to promote γ-TuSC binding to Spc110.
source: In this cell cycle phase Mps1 and Cdk1-Clb5 phosphorylate the N-terminus of Spc110 at five sites to promote γ-TuSC binding to Spc110 (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 10B showing a model diagram.

claim: Mps1 and Cdk1-Clb5 coordinate the timing of MT nucleation through Spc110 phosphorylation with SPB duplication.
source: We therefore suggest that Mps1 and Cdk1-Clb5 coordinate the timing of MT nucleation through Spc110 phosphorylation with SPB duplication.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Cdk1-Clb2 phosphorylation of Spc110T18 may limit the MT nucleation activity of the SPB associated γ-TuSC.
source: Thus, it is well possible that Spc110T18 phosphorylation by Cdk1-Clb2 limits the MT nucleation activity of the SPB associated γ-TuSC.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion.

claim: The yeast SPB of haploid cells organizes a constant number of 20 nuclear MTs during mitosis.
source: This model fits with the observation that the yeast SPB of haploid cells organizes a constant number of 20 nuclear MTs during mitosis (Winey et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to prior work.

claim: Co-overexpression of SPC97, SPC98, and TUB4 does not induce MT nucleation despite of γ-TuSC assembly.
source: Co-overexpression of SPC97, SPC98, and TUB4 does not induce MT nucleation despite of γ-TuSC assembly (Pereira et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to prior work.

claim: γ-TuSC binding to Spc110 and γ-TuSC oligomerization are mechanistically distinct steps.
source: We therefore suggest that γ-TuSC binding to Spc110 and TuSC oligomerization are mechanistically distinct steps (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion with reference to Figure 10C showing a model diagram.

claim: The N-terminal region of Spc98 exhibits homology to other GCP3 family members including human GCP3.
source: The N-terminal region of Spc98 exhibits homology to other GCP3 family members including human GCP3 (hGCP3, Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The N-Spc98 fragment was not essential for viability at 23°C.
source: Surprisingly, the N-Spc98 fragment was not essential for the viability at 23°C (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The special SPB arrangement of Spc110 as hexameric units compensates in part for the reduced in vitro binding of γ-TuSC(Spc98Δ1–156) to Spc110(1–220).
source: We suggest that the special SPB arrangement of Spc110 as hexameric units (Muller et al., 2005) compensates in part for the reduced in vitro binding of γ-TuSCSpc98Δ1–156 to Spc1101–220.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion with citation to prior work.

claim: Regions of γ-TuSC in addition to the N-terminal 177 amino acids of Spc98 have to interact with Spc110.
source: Whatever the mechanism, regions of γ-TuSC in addition to the N-terminal 177 amino acids of Spc98 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) have to interact with Spc110.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The CM1 motif was first identified in fission yeast Mto1.
source: This CM1 motif was first identified in fission yeast Mto1 (Sawin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to prior work.

claim: The function of CM1 in γ-TuSC binding was confirmed for Mto1, centrosomin (Drosophila), and CDK5RAP2 (human).
source: Subsequently the function of CM1 in γ-TuSC binding was confirmed for Mto1, centrosomin (Drosophila), and CDK5RAP2 (human) (Zhang and Megraw, 2007; Fong et al., 2008; Samejima et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: The γ-TuCRs Pcp1 (fission yeast) and Spc110 (budding yeast) also contain putative CM1 motifs.
source: The γ-TuCRs Pcp1 (fission yeast) and Spc110 (budding yeast) also contain putative CM1 motifs (Dictenberg et al., 1998; Takahashi et al., 2002; Zimmerman et al., 2004; Fong et al., 2010; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Human PCNT falls in terms of structure and function into the γ-TuCR class.
source: Human PCNT falls in terms of structure and function into the γ-TuCR class (Doxsey et al., 1994; Dictenberg et al., 1998; Gillingham and Munro, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Analysis of the PCNT sequence for CM1 in combination with the newly identified SPM identified a potential CM1 in the N-terminus of PCNT.
source: Analysis of the PCNT sequence for CM1 in combination with the newly identified SPM identified a potential CM1 in the N-terminus of PCNT (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 8B showing bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The γ-tubulin binding ability of human PCNT lies within the region that contains the SPM-CM1.
source: This is consistent with the γ-tubulin binding ability of human PCNT, which lies within the region that contains the SPM-CM1 (Takahashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to prior work.

claim: Super-resolution analysis of human centrosomes has mapped the localization of γ-tubulin towards the N-terminus of PCNT.
source: In addition, super-resolution analysis of human centrosomes has mapped the localization of γ-tubulin towards the N-terminus of PCNT (Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2012; Sonnen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: The SPM is important for Spc110 binding to γ-TuSC and induced oligomerization of γ-TuSC.
source: The SPM is important for Spc110 binding to γ-TuSC and induced oligomerization of γ-TuSC (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figures 3 and 4.

claim: SPM co-operates with CM1 to form a bipartite binding element for the γ-TuSC.
source: Based on these results we propose that SPM co-operates with CM1 to form a bipartite binding element for the γ-TuSC (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 10C showing a model diagram.

claim: The distance between SPM and CM1 is around 90–100 amino acids in the Spc110 and Pcp1 type of receptors.
source: The distance between SPM and CM1 is around 90–100 amino acids in the Spc110 and Pcp1 type of receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: In the mammalian PCNT subfamily, the distance between SPM and CM1 is around 70 amino acids.
source: In the mammalian PCNT subfamily it is however only around 70 amino acids.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: In budding and fission yeast, the CM1-MASC types of γ-TuCRs (Spc72 and Mto1) have specific functions in cytoplasmic MT organization.
source: In budding and fission yeast, the CM1-MASC types of γ-TuCRs (Spc72 and Mto1) have specific functions in cytoplasmic MT organization, while Spc110 and Pcp1 (SPM-CM1-PACT) organize only nuclear MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Spc110 and Pcp1 (SPM-CM1-PACT) organize only nuclear MTs in budding and fission yeast.
source: In budding and fission yeast, the CM1-MASC types of γ-TuCRs (Spc72 and Mto1) have specific functions in cytoplasmic MT organization, while Spc110 and Pcp1 (SPM-CM1-PACT) organize only nuclear MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Human CDK5RAP2, myomegalin (CM1–CM2 types), and pericentrin (SPM-CM1-PACT type) are associated with the centrosome.
source: Human CDK5RAP2, myomegalin (CM1–CM2 types), and pericentrin (SPM-CM1-PACT type) are associated with the centrosome (Doxsey et al., 1994; Fong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: CDK5RAP2 and myomegalin also have functions in acentrosomal MT nucleation for example MT nucleation by the Golgi.
source: However, CDK5RAP2 and myomegalin also have functions in acentrosomal MT nucleation for example MT nucleation by the Golgi (Choi et al., 2010; Roubin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Budding yeast organizes MTs only with γ-TuSC and γ-TuCRs.
source: Budding yeast organizes MTs only with γ-TuSC and γ-TuCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: GCP4 to 6 are not essential for MT nucleation in fission yeast and Drosophila.
source: However, GCP4 to 6 are not essential for MT nucleation in fission yeast and Drosophila, while GCP2/Alp4, GCP3/Alp6, and Mozart1 are essential for viability (Anders et al., 2006; Verollet et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: GCP2/Alp4, GCP3/Alp6, and Mozart1 are essential for viability in fission yeast and Drosophila.
source: However, GCP4 to 6 are not essential for MT nucleation in fission yeast and Drosophila, while GCP2/Alp4, GCP3/Alp6, and Mozart1 are essential for viability (Anders et al., 2006; Verollet et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to prior work.

claim: Fission yeast Mozart1 is essential for γ-TuSC recruitment to SPBs.
source: Puzzlingly, fission yeast Mozart1 is essential for γ-TuSC recruitment to SPBs (Masuda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to prior work.

claim: The basic principals of MT nucleation are conserved from yeast to human.
source: In any case, considering the conservation between the SPM and CM1 binding elements of γ-TuRCs and the N-terminal region of Spc98/GCP3, we suggest that the basic principals of MT nucleation are conserved from yeast to human.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.
